modalities.name: Fence-Rail Sketching
modalities.tagline: Quick sketches of real animals, drawing only what is actually there.
modalities.whatItIs: Fence-Rail Sketching is a new concept for small groups who stand at the rail of a farmyard pen with pencil and paper and make quick sketches of pigs, ducks or calves as they move about. No drawing skill is needed, because the point is looking: you draw the shape actually in front of you, not the animal you imagine.
modalities.coreIdea: The Ideal Parent Figure Protocol builds caring figures in the imagination; this pushes animal-assisted therapy the opposite way, toward a real animal seen exactly as it is, here and now. Every time the pencil starts drawing what a pig is supposed to look like, you look up again.
modalities.whatYouDo: With two or three others, a facilitator and the animals' keeper, you move slowly around the pen for about 45 minutes, making one-minute sketches whenever an animal turns, roots, preens or lies down. The facilitator asks only plain questions, such as where the ear really is, and never what the animal feels or what a drawing means. Sketches are not judged, and you keep them only if you want to.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who live much of the time inside their own heads, stories or worries and want an hour of plain looking. It might also appeal to anyone who likes animals but would rather not touch them or talk about themselves.
modalities.cautions: You stay outside the rail, but pigs can bite, calves can kick and ducks can peck or scratch, and farmyards are muddy and uneven, so keep the distance the keeper sets and watch your footing to avoid falls. Mention allergies or a fear of farm animals before booking, and the animals must always be free to move away.
modalities.tweet: Fence-Rail Sketching: pencils out at a farmyard pen, one-minute drawings of pigs, ducks and calves, and the only rule is to draw what is really there, not what you assume. An untested idea for anyone stuck in their head.

modalities.name: Curry Comb Partners
modalities.tagline: Pairs groom a calm horse, attention resting on brush and coat.
modalities.whatItIs: Curry Comb Partners is a proposed practice in which two people groom a calm horse or donkey together, under the eye of a trained handler. Instead of turning inward to explore feelings, attention goes outward into the hands: the brush, the coat, the animal's warmth and its small responses.
modalities.coreIdea: IFS turns attention inward, toward parts and their history; this takes animal work further outward, into simple shared care in the present. When inner commentary starts up, you go back to the next brush stroke instead of following it.
modalities.whatYouDo: You and a partner spend about 40 minutes grooming the same animal in a quiet stable, one on each side, working through brushing, combing the mane and wiping the face in a set order the handler shows you. You talk only as much as the task needs, and the handler watches the animal's comfort and tells you when to swap sides or stop. The session closes with both of you standing beside the animal for a few quiet breaths.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel crowded by their own thoughts and want a calm, hands-on task that pulls attention outward. It may also suit anyone who would like gentle company with another person without having to make conversation.
modalities.cautions: Horses and donkeys can startle, step on feet, bite, kick or knock you over in a fall, so you groom only animals the handler knows well, keep clear of the hind legs, watch your footing and stop when the animal shows it has had enough. Mention allergies to hair or dust and any fear of horses first, and remember that scratches from hooves or tack are possible too.
modalities.tweet: Forty quiet minutes, two brushes and one calm horse. Curry Comb Partners is a proposal for pairs who groom together under a handler's eye, with attention kept in the hands instead of the head.

modalities.name: Touch Without Names
modalities.tagline: Eyes closed, a keeper guides your hand to calm farm animals.
modalities.whatItIs: Touch Without Names is a new concept for small-group sessions at a farm sanctuary in which you sit with your eyes closed while a keeper guides your open hand onto calm animals, such as a sheep, a goat or a small pony. Nobody names the animal, describes it or asks you to guess: there is only coarse hair, springy fleece, warm skin and slight movement under your palm.
modalities.coreIdea: CBT names, labels and weighs experience in words; pushed the other way, animal work sets aside sight and names, so an animal is met only through touch. With nothing to identify, compare or judge, attention can rest on whatever the hand is feeling now.
modalities.whatYouDo: You and two or three others sit or kneel on low benches in a quiet straw pen for about 30 minutes, and one at a time a handler brings a calm animal to stand beside you while the keeper tells you only that your hand is about to touch, then rests it lightly on the animal's neck, shoulder or back. You keep your hand still or move it slowly, shifting and reaching a little as the animal moves, and there is no set order, number or sequence of animals. At the end everyone opens their eyes, looks at the animals they touched and sits for a few minutes before washing their hands.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who live inside a running commentary of naming, rating and analyzing, and who want time in contact with something alive that needs no words. It may also suit anyone who feels steadier through touch than through talk.
modalities.cautions: Only animals the keepers know to be calm with handling take part, each is held loosely at the head by its own handler and let go whenever it wants to move away, touches stay on the neck, shoulder or back and never near the legs or hindquarters, each animal rests between turns, and you keep your eyes closed only while seated and may open them at any moment. Animals can still bite, butt, tread on feet or pass on germs, so you wear sturdy boots, cover cuts, wash your hands afterward and mention allergies, a weakened immune system or a fear of animals before booking, and if closing your eyes feels uneasy you can keep them open with your gaze lowered.
modalities.tweet: What if you met a sheep, a goat and a pony by touch alone? In Touch Without Names, a new idea, you sit with eyes closed while a keeper rests your hand on calm animals. Open your eyes any time; animals are free to step away.

modalities.name: Silent Lead Rope
modalities.tagline: Lead a horse in silence, speaking only through posture and breath.
modalities.whatItIs: Silent Lead Rope is an untested idea for a nearly wordless session: you lead a calm horse through a simple course using only your posture, pace, breath and a loose rope. A professional and a horse handler guide every step with gestures rather than explanations.
modalities.coreIdea: ACT leans on words, metaphors and talk about values, so this version of animal work leaves language behind altogether. A horse tends to respond to clear, calm body signals rather than to what you say, which keeps attention in the body and the present moment.
modalities.whatYouDo: In a 45-minute session where the horse works in two short rounds of about ten minutes with a rest between, you lead it on a lead rope around an arena, asking it to start, stop, turn and pass through a gate, without speaking. The professional shows you each task with a gesture and steps in if anything becomes unsafe or the horse shows stress. At the end you have a few minutes to say one or two words about what you noticed, if you want to.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find talking about feelings hard, or who are tired of explaining themselves, and would rather learn by doing. It may also suit anyone curious about how much they communicate without words.
modalities.cautions: Leading a horse carries real risks of being stepped on, pulled, kicked or knocked down in a fall, so it needs a calm, well-trained horse, sturdy shoes and a handler within reach, and the horse rests between rounds and stops working at the first sign of stress. Mention allergies or a fear of horses before starting, and remember that bites and scratches can happen even with calm animals.
modalities.tweet: I keep coming back to this one: lead a calm horse through gates and turns without a single word, using only posture and breath. Silent Lead Rope is untested, with a handler beside you and rests for the horse. 🐴

modalities.name: Pottering With Hens
modalities.tagline: Slow, aimless garden pottering while friendly hens scratch around you.
modalities.whatItIs: Pottering With Hens is a new concept for unhurried time in a walled garden or orchard where a flock of tame hens forages freely, while you and a few others potter about with small, easy jobs. A keeper is there throughout, and nothing needs to be figured out, finished or talked about.
modalities.coreIdea: Coherence Therapy brings hidden emotional learnings vividly to the surface so they can be understood; this heads the other way, toward settling, with nothing to figure out. Slow, small jobs alongside contented animals are the whole practice.
modalities.whatYouDo: For about an hour you pull a few weeds, rake a path, sit on an upturned crate or simply stand and watch, while the hens peck and wander around your feet. The keeper shows you how to move slowly so the hens stay relaxed, and if one comes close you can watch it or offer an open palm. There is no topic to discuss, no feeding round to finish and no target for the garden.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel wound up or stuck in analyzing everything and want an hour that is slow and practical by design. It might also appeal to anyone who wants gentle animal company without large animals.
modalities.cautions: Hens can peck, which is a bird's bite, and scratch, and their droppings can carry germs such as salmonella, so wear gloves, wash your hands afterward and pick a hen up only if the keeper shows you how, and the hens are always free to wander off and are never chased. Mention allergies to feathers or dust and any fear of birds first, and watch your footing on uneven ground to avoid falls.
modalities.tweet: Pottering With Hens: an hour in a walled garden doing small jobs that hardly matter while tame hens scratch about your feet. A new idea for minds that insist on analyzing everything.

modalities.name: Writing the Dog's Profile
modalities.tagline: A small group meets a shelter dog, then writes its adoption profile.
modalities.whatItIs: Writing the Dog's Profile is a new concept for small groups who spend time with one dog waiting for a home at a rescue shelter and then write its adoption profile together, guided by a staff member who knows the dog. The task turns careful watching and careful words into something that matters to the dog's future.
modalities.coreIdea: TRE works through the body, alone and without words; moving away from it, this puts words, discussion and other people at the center. Finding true, kind and accurate words for a real animal in front of you is the whole practice.
modalities.whatYouDo: Four to six people sit in a quiet room for about an hour while a handler brings in one calm shelter dog, and for the first half you watch it, play a little if it wants and note what you see. For the second half the group drafts a short profile together, debating each phrase until it is both honest and kind, and the staff member checks it against what they know. The finished profile goes up on the shelter's adoption page.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who like words and want a sociable, useful task that keeps them in the present. It could also suit anyone who loves dogs but cannot adopt one.
modalities.cautions: Mention allergies or a fear of dogs before joining, and remember that shelter dogs can be anxious and may bite or scratch, so staff choose calm dogs, the handler stays in charge and the dog leaves for a rest whenever it shows stress. Staff have the last word on what the profile says about the dog's needs.
modalities.tweet: Suppose a shelter dog's chance of a home depended on your words. Writing the Dog's Profile is an untested idea: a small group meets one dog, watches it closely and writes its adoption profile together.

modalities.name: Reading Ears and Tails
modalities.tagline: Learn to read an animal's yes, no and maybe before touching.
modalities.whatItIs: Reading Ears and Tails is a new concept for a guided small-group course in reading animal body language, taught by a professional with calm dogs or horses. You learn to spot signs of comfort, worry and interest, and to ask an animal for contact and read its answer.
modalities.coreIdea: Focusing teaches patient attention to your own vague bodily sense of things; this turns the same patience outward, to another body's signals, with a professional guiding. Asking before touching, and respecting a no, is practiced as a real skill.
modalities.whatYouDo: In 60-minute sessions with three or four others, you watch a calm animal while the professional points out ears, tail, eyes, weight shifts and yawns, and what each might mean. You then take turns offering a hand at a respectful distance and saying aloud whether you read a yes, a no or a maybe, and the handler confirms or corrects you. Over several weeks the animals and their signals become more varied.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who want to feel more confident and safe around animals, and anyone who wants to practice consent and boundaries in a concrete, low-stakes way. It could also interest people who find other people's moods hard to read.
modalities.cautions: Even calm animals can bite, scratch or kick when their signals are missed, and a startled horse can knock you over in a fall, so only work with trained animals and handlers and keep to the distances you are shown, and let the animal move away whenever it chooses. Mention allergies or a fear of animals first, and take what you learn as a guide rather than a certainty, since signals vary between animals.
modalities.tweet: Could you tell when a dog means no? An animal's yes, no and maybe, learned before anyone touches, is what Reading Ears and Tails would teach in a proposed small-group course with a professional.

modalities.name: The Morning Feed Round
modalities.tagline: A fixed morning routine caring for real animals' real needs.
modalities.whatItIs: The Morning Feed Round is an invented practice in which you join a keeper at a farm or animal sanctuary and work through the same set morning routine on every visit: feeding, fresh water, checking each animal and cleaning. The animals depend on the job being done, which makes the practice concrete and practical rather than reflective.
modalities.coreIdea: Aletheia Coaching follows whatever unfolds inside you, with few fixed steps; going the other way, this is an outward, step-by-step task with a clear result. Being trusted with real needs, in the same order every time, is the heart of it.
modalities.whatYouDo: Once or twice a week you arrive early, sign in and spend about an hour working through a checklist the keeper has written for your group of two or three people. You top up water, refill hay nets, check that each animal is eating and moving normally, sweep the yard and note what you did, while the keeper does any heavy lifting. The keeper goes over the checklist with you before you leave and adds one new task when you are ready.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel adrift and want a reliable routine with a visible purpose, for example during unemployment, after retirement or after a hard period. It may also suit anyone who would rather do something useful with their hands than talk.
modalities.cautions: Farmyards have slippery floors, tools and animals that can push, kick, bite or scratch, and falls are common, so the keeper should train and supervise you, keep you away from heavy lifting and match tasks to your fitness, and the animals are never chased, cornered or handled without the keeper. Wash your hands after animal contact, and mention allergies, a fear of any of the animals or health conditions beforehand.
modalities.tweet: Animals waiting for you at nine is a good reason to get up. The Morning Feed Round: one hour, the same checklist each visit, a keeper doing the heavy lifting. An untested idea for adrift weeks.

modalities.name: Team Search Practice
modalities.tagline: A small team plans searches with a trained scent dog, then reviews.
modalities.whatItIs: Team Search Practice is a new concept for a structured group program in which teams of three or four work with a trained search dog and its handler, hiding scented toys in a field or barn and planning how to search for them. Each session has a set goal, a plan, the search and a review, so the focus is on working together toward a clear result.
modalities.coreIdea: Do Nothing meditation drops every goal and lets go of control. Its opposite here is a shared plan, a measurable result and deliberate change in how the team cooperates, with a dog whose nose shows at once whether the plan was any good.
modalities.whatYouDo: Each session lasts about an hour: the team hides a few scented toys, agrees a search pattern on a sketch map and then walks it with the dog and handler, taking turns to hold the long line. The dog searches in short bursts of a few minutes with rests and water in between, and afterward the professional leads a review of what the team planned against what happened. Over six to eight weeks the hides get harder and the team takes on more of the planning.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who want to practice teamwork, planning or leadership in a concrete way, such as a youth group, a work team or a recovery group. It could also work for anyone who learns better by doing than by discussing.
modalities.cautions: Mention allergies or a fear of dogs first, and remember that an excited working dog can bite, scratch or pull someone off balance into a fall, so the handler keeps control of the dog, the line and the pace. The dog works only in short bursts, rests often and stops at once if it seems tired or stressed.
modalities.tweet: Plan it, search it, review it, with a trained search dog whose nose shows at once whether the plan worked. Team Search Practice is a new concept, untested so far, for teams that learn by doing.

modalities.name: The Unearned Welcome
modalities.tagline: Let a friendly dog's welcome reach you without trying to earn it.
modalities.whatItIs: The Unearned Welcome is an untested idea for small-group visits with friendly, trained dogs, where the only task is to notice being greeted. Instead of producing kind feelings on purpose, you let real warmth arrive from a real animal and see what happens.
modalities.coreIdea: Metta builds goodwill by repeating phrases toward people you picture in your mind; this reverses the direction, toward receiving warmth that is really there, with no phrases and no effort. Being welcomed without having done anything to earn it is the core experience.
modalities.whatYouDo: You and four or five others walk slowly around a large, fenced garden for about 45 minutes while two or three friendly dogs roam free with their handler and greet whoever they choose; nobody steers them toward anyone. When a dog comes to you, you can stroke it, let it lean against you or simply notice the welcome, and the professional invites you to notice whatever comes up, awkwardness included, without needing to say it. The session closes with a short round where anyone can share one moment that stood out.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find it hard to accept kindness, or who feel they must earn every bit of affection. It may also appeal to anyone who finds loving-kindness phrases forced and wants something more direct.
modalities.cautions: Being welcomed warmly can stir up sadness or old feelings of not being wanted, so the professional should be ready to slow things down and suggest further support. Mention allergies or a fear of dogs first, and remember that excited greetings can bring a scratch, a bite or a stumble, so the handlers keep greetings calm.
modalities.tweet: Hard to accept kindness? Try a garden of friendly trained dogs who greet whoever they like. The Unearned Welcome, still untested, asks only that you notice being welcomed.

modalities.name: A Slow Animal Friendship
modalities.tagline: Get to know one animal, visit after visit, in a small group.
modalities.whatItIs: A Slow Animal Friendship is a new concept for a ten-week program in which a small group visits the same animal, such as a sanctuary goat, pony or dog, at the same time each week. The point is a growing relationship: learning one animal's habits, likes and history, and letting it get to know you.
modalities.coreIdea: Vipassana watches each experience arise and pass, alone and in silence; this goes toward a relationship that continues and deepens over time, shared with others. Continuity, rather than a single moment, is what the practice builds.
modalities.whatYouDo: Each week you spend about an hour with your group and the same animal, guided by its handler: you sit with it, notice what has changed, offer the play or attention it enjoys and swap stories about it. The professional keeps a light thread running between sessions, such as what you learned last time and what you are curious about now. There is no set program, and the friendship simply grows at the animal's pace.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find relationships hard to sustain, or who are rebuilding trust, and want a gentle, predictable bond to practice with. It might also appeal to anyone who would like a weekly fixed point that involves both people and an animal.
modalities.cautions: Endings can be hard, so the program should prepare for the last visit from the start and point people to support if it brings up grief, and if the animal is unwell or stressed the session changes or stops. Mention allergies or a fear of animals first, and remember the risks of bites and scratches, and with a pony kicks and falls, which the handler manages by staying close.
modalities.tweet: Ten weeks with the same sanctuary goat. A Slow Animal Friendship is a proposed small-group program for getting to know one animal at its own pace: the habits, the moods, the favorite scratch.

modalities.name: Shared Siesta
modalities.tagline: Rest or doze while a calm dog naps nearby; nothing is asked.
modalities.whatItIs: Shared Siesta is a proposed practice of shared rest: a handler brings a calm dog to someone who is in bed or in a chair, at home, in hospital or in a care home, and the dog naps on its own blanket nearby while the person rests too. There is no task, no exercise and no need to talk or to touch the dog.
modalities.coreIdea: HIIT pushes the body to its limit in timed bursts; this goes as far the other way as it can, to complete stillness, calm and acceptance. Resting in company is the whole activity, not a gap between efforts.
modalities.whatYouDo: At a set rest time, such as early afternoon, the handler settles the dog on a blanket a short distance from your bed or chair, dims the lights if you like and sits quietly nearby for about 30 minutes. You can doze, watch the dog sleep or chat softly with the handler, but you let the sleeping dog lie and stroke it only if it wakes and comes to you. The visit ends when you wake or the time is up, with no plan for next time unless you want one.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who are ill, recovering, very tired or living with limited mobility, for whom most activities ask too much right now. It could also suit anyone who rests better with a calm presence nearby.
modalities.cautions: Touching a sleeping dog can startle it into a bite or scratch, so the dog rests out of reach unless it wakes and approaches, and the handler stays awake and in charge of it throughout. Skip visits with allergies, a fear of dogs, a weakened immune system or open wounds unless the care team agrees, and follow the setting's hygiene rules.
modalities.tweet: On days when moving is too much, a calm dog could simply nap on its own blanket near your bed while you rest. That is all of Shared Siesta, an idea for illness and exhaustion, with no petting needed.

modalities.name: Watching the Fish
modalities.tagline: A still half hour alone in front of a large aquarium.
modalities.whatItIs: Watching the Fish is a new concept for quiet, near-solitary sessions in which you sit in front of a large, well-kept aquarium and simply watch the fish, with a professional sitting quietly at the back of the room. Thoughts and memories are free to drift in, and you can talk them over with the professional at the end if you want to.
modalities.coreIdea: Team sport is loud, fast and full of other people to read and react to; at the opposite pole, this is a still, almost private session with creatures that ask nothing of you. Slow, silent movement behind glass gives the eyes something real to rest on.
modalities.whatYouDo: You sit in a soft chair in a dim, quiet room for about 30 minutes, watching the fish turn, hover and feed, with no task and no phone. The professional stays at a desk at the back and speaks only if you ask, and for the last ten minutes you can say what came to mind, or nothing at all. Sessions can run weekly for a few weeks.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel crowded and overstimulated by others, or who are not ready to talk, and want the quietest possible start. It could also suit people who are allergic to or nervous around furry animals.
modalities.cautions: There is no handling, so allergies, bites and scratches are not a concern as long as nobody touches the tank water, but anyone with a fear of fish or deep water should say so first, and the aquarium must be properly kept so the fish are not stressed by light, noise or tapping. Memories that drift in can be painful, so the professional should be trained to respond; the session uses only memories you already have, treats images and feelings that surface as experiences rather than evidence of what happened, and is never used to uncover forgotten events.
modalities.tweet: Thirty minutes, one big aquarium and nobody asking anything of you. Watching the Fish is a hypothetical session for overstimulated days, with a professional sitting quietly at the back in case you want to talk.

modalities.name: Sitting With Old Dogs
modalities.tagline: Slow company with retired old dogs, and talk about slowing down.
modalities.whatItIs: Sitting With Old Dogs is a new concept for small, seated group sessions at a sanctuary or shelter for old, retired dogs, led by a professional and a carer. You spend time with dogs who now move slowly and sleep a lot, and the group talks about rest, limits and slowing down in your own life.
modalities.coreIdea: Endurance training is about going further and keeping going; this turns it around toward stopping, resting and accepting limits, shared with others and guided. Elderly dogs, who no longer push on, set the pace and the theme.
modalities.whatYouDo: Once a week, four to six people sit on low chairs in a quiet room for about an hour while two or three old dogs wander between them, settle or sleep. For the first half you simply keep them company, stroking a dog that comes to you, and for the second half the professional opens a short conversation, such as what you find hard to stop doing. Each session follows the same shape, and the dogs are never woken or moved to suit the group.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find it hard to rest, slow down or accept limits, such as after an injury, a burnout or a change in health. It could also suit anyone who loves old dogs and their unhurried company.
modalities.cautions: Old dogs tire quickly and may have sore joints, and a drowsy or sore dog that is touched may bite or scratch, so contact stays gentle and brief and sleeping dogs are left alone. Mention allergies or a fear of dogs first, and since the talk may touch on aging or loss, the professional should be ready to offer more support.
modalities.tweet: Old dogs are experts at slowing down, so why not learn from them? Call it Sitting With Old Dogs: a proposed weekly group that keeps retired dogs company, then talks with a professional about rest and limits.

modalities.name: Featherweight Holding
modalities.tagline: Practice gentleness by holding a small, calm animal on your lap.
modalities.whatItIs: Featherweight Holding is an untested idea for small-group sessions in which each person gently holds a small, calm animal on a lap blanket, such as a guinea pig, a hen or a small dog used to handling, guided by a handler. The theme is gentleness: how lightly you can hold something alive and fragile, and how it feels to do so.
modalities.coreIdea: Strength training moves heavy loads with effort and control; this explores the reverse, the lightest possible touch, stillness and letting go of control. The animal's comfort is the measure of how gentle you are being.
modalities.whatYouDo: You sit with four or five others in a calm room for about 30 minutes while the handler shows each person how to support an animal on a blanket on their lap. Each animal is held for no more than five minutes before going back to its pen to rest, and if it shows it wants to move sooner, you let it go. The professional invites quiet conversation about gentleness, including being gentle with yourself, and nobody has to speak.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who are hard on themselves or always in control, and who want to practice softness in a very concrete way. It may also suit older adults or anyone with limited strength, since nothing heavy is involved.
modalities.cautions: Small animals are easily stressed or hurt and can bite or scratch when frightened, so only animals that tolerate handling take part, holds are brief and the handler stops at any sign of unease. Mention allergies or a fear of animals first, and wash your hands afterward to lower the risk of infection.
modalities.tweet: Strength training rewards force. Featherweight Holding rewards the lightest touch you can manage: a small, calm animal on your lap for five minutes, held as gently as possible. A new concept in softness.

modalities.name: Who Grooms Whom
modalities.tagline: Watch a herd's friendships unfold, then talk about your own.
modalities.whatItIs: Who Grooms Whom is a new concept for small-group visits to a field of horses or goats with a keeper, watching the herd's real social life: who grazes beside whom, who grooms whom, who keeps apart. The group then talks about what it saw and what it brings to mind about friendship and belonging.
modalities.coreIdea: Qigong works on your own body through a set, repeated form; this leans the other way, toward open-ended attention to the relationships of other creatures, shared in conversation. The talk stays tied to what the group actually saw happen in the field.
modalities.whatYouDo: You stroll slowly along the edge of the field with a keeper and three to six others for about 90 minutes, stopping to watch pairs and small groups as they graze, groom each other, play or move apart. The keeper explains what the behavior usually means for that species, and every so often the group talks for a few minutes about what stood out and whether it echoes anything in their own lives. There is no set structure beyond the walk, and no one has to share anything personal.
modalities.whoItsFor: People thinking about friendship, loneliness or belonging who find it easier to start from something they can see. It could also suit animal lovers who want a gentle, sociable outing.
modalities.cautions: You watch from outside the fence or at a distance the keeper sets, since horses and goats can bite, scratch, kick or knock a person over, and the ground may be uneven, so wear sturdy shoes to avoid falls. Mention allergies or a fear of animals first, and since talk about friendship can touch sore spots, the keeper should know where to point people for support.
modalities.tweet: Who stands next to whom in a herd, and who always stands alone? Watch the real friendships in a field of horses or goats with a keeper, then talk about your own. Working title: Who Grooms Whom. Untested.

modalities.name: Lift, Look, Lower
modalities.tagline: A slow one-to-one hive check, done in the same fixed order.
modalities.whatItIs: Lift, Look, Lower is a new concept for one-to-one sessions with an experienced beekeeper, who opens a honeybee hive so that you can lift out its frames one by one in a fixed order, look at each and put it back. It borrows the steps of an ordinary hive inspection, but beyond how to hold a frame nothing is taught, recorded or decided: the session is built around slowness and the same sequence every week, not around learning to keep bees.
modalities.coreIdea: Socializing means many people, quick talk and whatever happens next; moving away from it, this is one guide, one task and the same short sequence of slow movements every time. Bees tend to stay calmer around slow, steady handling, so each careful lift keeps the body unhurried and attention on what is in front of you.
modalities.whatYouDo: Your first visit is spent only sitting a few meters from the hive watching bees come and go, and the hive work starts once being near them feels calm. After a sting-allergy check and a fitting for a full suit, veil and gloves, the beekeeper uses the smoker and lifts the lid on a warm, calm day, and you lift out each frame in turn, hold it over the open hive for about half a minute while you look at the bees, honey and brood, and lower it back, with the beekeeper beside you stepping in only when needed. The hive is closed within about fifteen minutes, you finish by sitting to one side watching the entrance, and you return to the same hive each week through the warm months.
modalities.whoItsFor: People drained by noise, talk and social demands who want a calm, absorbing session with one other person and a single slow task. It may also suit anyone who settles best with a clear sequence of hands-on steps.
modalities.cautions: Stings happen even in a suit, so anyone with a known sting allergy or a past severe reaction should not take part, people with heart conditions should check with a doctor first, and the beekeeper keeps a phone and an emergency plan at hand, closes the hive and moves you away at the first sign of a strong reaction or defensive bees. For the colony's sake the hive is opened only on warm, dry, calm days, at most once a week and only briefly; suits get hot, so drink water, and mention any fear of insects before booking.
modalities.tweet: Ever looked inside a beehive? Lift, Look, Lower is a new idea: one-to-one sessions with a beekeeper, lifting out each frame slowly in the same order every week. Not for anyone allergic to stings.

modalities.name: Puzzle Feeder Workshop
modalities.tagline: Build puzzle feeders for sanctuary animals indoors, then watch them used.
modalities.whatItIs: Puzzle Feeder Workshop is a new concept for structured indoor sessions at a farm sanctuary, where a small group builds simple enrichment toys for the animals, such as rooting boxes for pigs and hay puzzles for goats, following step-by-step instructions from staff. At the end of each session you watch the animals work out what you made.
modalities.coreIdea: Nature walks are open, outdoors and self-led; this brings animal work indoors, into a room with a clear method and a trained guide. Making something with your hands for an animal that will really use it gives each session a concrete purpose.
modalities.whatYouDo: Once a week, four to six people meet in a sanctuary workroom for about 90 minutes and follow a set plan: a short demonstration, an hour of cutting, knotting and filling, and a clean-up. Staff then put one or two of the new toys in a pen while the group watches from behind the rail, and the professional leads a short talk about patience and care. Over the weeks the designs get a little harder.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who like practical, hands-on tasks and want to do something useful for animals in a calm, structured setting. It could also suit those who cannot easily get outdoors or who prefer a predictable indoor routine.
modalities.cautions: Pigs and goats can bite, scratch or butt, so the group watches from behind a rail, staff do all the handling, and the toys use only materials staff have checked are safe for the animals. Mention allergies or a fear of animals first, and take care with scissors and other tools.
modalities.tweet: Pigs get bored too. Build them rooting boxes and hay puzzles at a farm sanctuary, then watch them work it out: that is the new idea behind Puzzle Feeder Workshop, calm and hands-on.

modalities.name: Lost Companion Walks
modalities.tagline: Small group walks with therapy dogs for people grieving a pet.
modalities.whatItIs: Lost Companion Walks is a proposed format for small group walks for people who have lost a pet, led by a trained grief counselor or mental health clinician, with one or two calm therapy dogs and their handler along. You walk, take turns holding a lead if you want to, and talk with others who understand that this kind of grief is real.
modalities.coreIdea: Sensory mindfulness keeps quiet, solitary attention on present sensation; this goes toward company, conversation and memory, shared on the move. Walking beside a living dog can make it easier to talk about one who has died, without having to sit face to face.
modalities.whatYouDo: Once a week for six weeks, four to eight people meet the counselor and a handler with one or two calm dogs for a 45-minute walk on a quiet, level route. Along the way you can share stories about the animal you lost, walk a stretch holding a dog's lead or simply listen, and the counselor offers one gentle prompt each week, such as a favorite memory or a habit you miss. The dogs get water and rest stops along the way, and the handler takes a dog out of the walk if it seems tired or stressed.
modalities.whoItsFor: People grieving a pet who feel that friends and family do not quite understand the loss. It could also suit people who stopped going out after losing a dog and want a gentle way back outdoors.
modalities.cautions: Being around dogs can bring grief to the surface, so anyone can walk without a dog, step away or leave early, the counselor should refer people whose grief stays overwhelming to further support, and the walks share only memories people already have, never treat feelings or images as evidence of what happened and are never used to recover forgotten events. Mention allergies or a fear of dogs first, and remember that dogs can bite, scratch or pull you off balance into a fall, so the handler keeps leads short, limits how many people take turns and keeps routes level.
modalities.tweet: Grieving a pet can be lonely when others think it was just an animal. Lost Companion Walks, a proposed weekly walk led by a grief counselor with calm therapy dogs along, makes room for that loss.

modalities.name: Hay and Hoof Listening
modalities.tagline: Sit quietly in a stable and listen to the animals, not music.
modalities.whatItIs: Hay and Hoof Listening is a new concept for guided listening sessions in a barn or stable at feeding time, where you sit and listen to the animals instead of to music. Chewing, breathing, shifting hooves and soft calls become the only soundtrack.
modalities.coreIdea: Music shapes sound to carry emotion and expression; here the sound is unarranged and alive, and you only receive it. A guide gives the listening a simple shape, but nothing is performed or expressed.
modalities.whatYouDo: You and a few others sit on hay bales or chairs in a stable for about 40 minutes while a guide leads a short listening sequence: sounds close by, sounds further away, then the quiet between them. Afterward you can walk slowly along the stalls with the handler, greet the animals and say a few words about what you heard. Phones stay off and no music is played.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find silence uncomfortable but music too emotionally loaded, and want something calm and real to listen to. It could also interest anyone who enjoys the atmosphere of barns and stables.
modalities.cautions: Stables are dusty and full of allergens, so people with asthma or allergies should check first, and anyone with a fear of horses should say so. You stay where the handler places you, out of reach of teeth and hooves, because a horse can bite, kick, scratch you against a wall or knock you into a fall, and you wear sturdy shoes and keep quiet at feeding time so the animals can eat undisturbed.
modalities.tweet: Ever listened to a stable at feeding time? Chewing, breathing, a hoof shifting in straw. Forty minutes on a hay bale, guided from near sounds to far ones, would be Hay and Hoof Listening. Still untested.

modalities.name: The Unpictured Routine
modalities.tagline: A steady, picture-free routine: only weight, stretch and warmth.
modalities.whatItIs: The Unpictured Routine is a new concept for a fixed, self-taught movement routine practiced with no imagery at all, in which you say aloud one plain word for what you feel at each movement, such as heavy, stretch or warm. It takes steady, warming effort, a step up from slow, gentle forms, with deep knee bends, long reaches and steps.
modalities.coreIdea: The Ideal Parent Figure Protocol is therapist-led, rich in imagined scenes and reaches far into the past; this pushes qigong the other way, to a self-led, purely physical routine anchored in the present. If an image or memory appears, you let it go and return to what the body is sensing.
modalities.whatYouDo: Standing in any open spot, indoors or out, you work through eight movements, such as sinking into a deep knee bend, reaching high and wide, turning at the waist and stepping forward and back, for about 25 minutes, enough to feel warm. At each movement you say one real sensation word out loud, and if an image or story starts instead, you replace it with the next plain word. You do it alone, with no teacher, music or recording.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find visualization frustrating, or who want a body practice with nothing to imagine and nothing to believe and a little more effort than gentle forms. It may also suit anyone who wants a simple routine they can start alone today.
modalities.cautions: Warm up with a few minutes of easy movement, build up the depth of the bends gradually, adapt any movement that strains your knees, back or balance, get medical advice first if you have a heart or joint problem, and stop if you feel chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness. The routine never works with memories: any images or memories that appear are not evidence of anything and are never followed in search of forgotten events, and if strong ones or unusual sensations keep coming up, or you have a history of psychosis, talk to a doctor or an experienced teacher before going on.
modalities.tweet: Qigong without the imagery: no glowing energy balls, no rivers of light. The Unpictured Routine is a new concept where you say one plain word aloud for what you feel, through 25 minutes of steady movement.

modalities.name: The Single Step
modalities.tagline: One step forward and back, repeated until the body is warm.
modalities.whatItIs: The Single Step is an untested idea for a practice made of one movement: you step forward and push both palms out as you breathe out, then step back and draw them in as you breathe in, again and again, for about 20 minutes, changing legs every few minutes. It is as simple and repetitive as a practice can be, yet steady enough to warm you a little, and after one demonstration it can be done alone anywhere.
modalities.coreIdea: IFS explores many inner voices and their histories with a therapist; this pares qigong down to one movement, one rhythm and one point of attention, done on your own. Total repetition leaves nothing to choose, analyze or negotiate.
modalities.whatYouDo: You stand in a clear space and repeat the step and push at an even pace set by your natural breath, switching the leading leg every few minutes and adding a little time each week if it feels easy. A timer ends the session, so there is nothing to count or keep track of. Done daily, it becomes a fixed ritual with a clear beginning and end.
modalities.whoItsFor: People whose minds feel crowded with competing voices and who want something utterly simple to do, with enough effort to keep the body busy. It might also appeal to those who like clear, repeatable routines.
modalities.cautions: Start with a few easy steps as a warm-up, keep the steps short if your knees, hips or balance are unsteady, practice on a non-slip floor, breathe easily rather than forcing it and stop if you feel chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness or your joints hurt. Check with a doctor first if you have a heart, joint or balance condition, and anyone with a history of psychosis or another serious mental illness should get medical advice before taking up a repetitive meditative practice.
modalities.tweet: One step forward with a push of the palms, one step back, for twenty minutes. The Single Step is a proposal for crowded minds, with nothing to choose and nothing to analyze.

modalities.name: Slow Housework Round
modalities.tagline: The same chores, same order, done slowly in time with the breath.
modalities.whatItIs: Slow Housework Round is a new concept for turning a fixed set of real chores into a movement practice: sweeping one floor, wiping one table, folding a basket of washing and watering the plants, always in the same order and always slowly, in time with the breath. There is nothing to think through and nothing to get right beyond the next movement.
modalities.coreIdea: CBT works on thoughts by examining and testing them; pushed away from it, qigong becomes all body and no argument, with steady light effort and an accepting attitude. Thoughts that come up are neither disputed nor followed, and attention returns to the hands.
modalities.whatYouDo: After a minute of loosening your shoulders and hips, you spend about 25 minutes working through your round, making each broom stroke, wipe of the cloth or fold slowly and breathing out as you move. If you catch yourself rushing or judging how well it is done, you slow down and return to the next movement. You finish by standing still in the tidied room for a few breaths.
modalities.whoItsFor: People whose minds race and who find that thinking-based techniques make them more alert, and who would rather do something useful than sit still. It could also suit anyone who wants a practice that fits into ordinary chores.
modalities.cautions: Warm up first, keep your back long, switch hands often and bend from the knees for low jobs, wear a mask if the area is dusty and skip wet or slippery floors. People with back or shoulder problems should choose light tasks and stop if anything hurts, anyone should stop and sit down if they feel chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness, and anyone with a history of psychosis should get medical advice before taking up slow, breath-led practice.
modalities.tweet: Slow Housework Round turns the chores into the practice: sweep, wipe, fold and water in the same order every time, slowly and with the breath. An untested idea for racing minds.

modalities.name: Toes to Crown
modalities.tagline: Every joint moved in order, from the toes up to the crown.
modalities.whatItIs: Toes to Crown is an invented routine, a completely fixed sequence that moves every joint in the body in order, from the toes up to the neck, and then links them in a few full-body movements. It is learned once from a teacher or a printed chart and then practiced alone, exactly the same every time.
modalities.coreIdea: ACT is flexible, conversational and full of metaphor; at the other extreme sits a literal, wordless, fully mapped routine. Knowing exactly what comes next is part of the appeal.
modalities.whatYouDo: Standing, or seated if you need to, you make eight slow circles with each joint in turn (toes, ankles, knees, hips, spine, shoulders, elbows, wrists, fingers and neck), then link them in three full-body movements: a deep squat, a long lunge to each side and a reach overhead, eight times each. A full round takes about 30 minutes and leaves you pleasantly warm. You always finish by standing still for one minute.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who like order and predictability and want a thorough daily routine they never have to think about. It may also suit those whose minds get busy when instructions are vague.
modalities.cautions: Let the toe and ankle circles warm you up before the squats and lunges, make small, pain-free circles, shrink or skip any joint that is injured or arthritic, keep squats and lunges shallow at first, use the seated version if your balance is unsteady and stop if you feel chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness. Keep neck circles slow and partial, check with a doctor or physiotherapist first if you have a neck, spine, heart or joint condition, and get medical advice first if you have a history of psychosis.
modalities.tweet: Proposal: Toes to Crown, a fixed routine that circles every joint in order from the toes up, then links them in squats, lunges and reaches. The same thirty minutes every day, for anyone who likes knowing what comes next.

modalities.name: The Four Surfaces
modalities.tagline: One short form, done barefoot on four different kinds of ground.
modalities.whatItIs: The Four Surfaces is a new concept for practicing one short, breath-led qigong-style form barefoot on four different patches of ground in turn, such as grass, sand, smooth paving and a rubber mat. The form never changes; only the ground does, and you notice how each surface changes the same movements.
modalities.coreIdea: Coherence Therapy brings strong, hidden emotional learnings to the surface to find the meaning in them; this heads toward deep settling, with no meaning to find, only the plain feel of different ground underfoot. The same form on changing surfaces keeps attention in the feet and legs.
modalities.whatYouDo: In a garden, park corner or yard where four surfaces sit close together, you do a five-minute form of long, slow steps, deep weight shifts and low bends on each one in the same order, for about 25 minutes in all, which is steady enough to leave you warm. Between surfaces you stand still for a few breaths and notice what is different, such as softer, colder or more slippery. You practice alone, choosing the patches once and keeping them the same.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel keyed up or overwhelmed by emotion-focused work and want something purely physical and steady. It could also work for anyone who likes being outdoors but wants a set practice rather than a walk.
modalities.cautions: Check each surface for glass, stones, heat or ice before you start, skip barefoot practice if you have diabetes, poor circulation or foot wounds, keep the steps small on slippery ground, begin with a few minutes of easy stepping and stop if you feel chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness. Check with a doctor first if you have a heart, joint or balance condition, and people with a history of psychosis or another serious mental illness should get medical advice before starting meditative movement practice.
modalities.tweet: How does the same movement change on sand instead of tiles? The Four Surfaces sets out to find out: one short form done barefoot on four different grounds, with nothing to interpret. A new idea.

modalities.name: Not One Jingle
modalities.tagline: Move so smoothly that small bells on your wrists never ring.
modalities.whatItIs: Not One Jingle is a proposed movement form practiced with a small bell tied loosely to each wrist, in which you move so smoothly and steadily that neither bell makes a sound. Every movement is continuous, with no jerks, sudden stops or trembling, and the bells tell you at once when one slips through. It borrows a children's classroom game, carrying a bell without letting it ring, and stretches it into a whole slow movement form for adults.
modalities.coreIdea: TRE invites the body to shake and tremble on its own; this takes qigong the opposite way, toward deliberate smoothness, control and calm. Steady, unbroken motion is the whole aim, and the bells make it something you can hear.
modalities.whatYouDo: After learning the form in a few classes, you practice at home for about 20 minutes, moving your arms through slow lifts, turns and circles while stepping gently and listening for any ring. When a bell sounds, you pause, soften and carry on more slowly, without counting or scoring the rings. A teacher or practice partner can watch from time to time and point out where movements could flow more evenly.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel jittery or shaky under stress and want to practice the opposite: smooth, deliberate movement. It may also suit those who like a clear standard to aim for.
modalities.cautions: Keep the knees soft and the steps small to protect your balance, tie the bells loosely so nothing tightens on the wrist and practice on a clear floor. If you have a tremor from a medical condition, leave the bells off or treat silence as a direction rather than a test, and anyone with a history of psychosis or another serious mental illness should get medical advice before taking up meditative movement practice.
modalities.tweet: Jittery under stress? Tie a small bell to each wrist and move through slow lifts and turns so smoothly that neither one rings. Not One Jingle takes about 20 minutes a day and is still just an idea.

modalities.name: Mirror and Plumb Line
modalities.tagline: A precise form practiced at a mirror, correcting alignment each time.
modalities.whatItIs: Mirror and Plumb Line is a new concept for practicing a precise movement form in front of a full-length mirror with a vertical line marked down it, checking and correcting your alignment as you go. The form uses low stances, long steps and full reaches, so it takes steady effort, and each posture should match the reference a teacher showed you.
modalities.coreIdea: Focusing waits patiently for a vague inner felt sense to form; this replaces the waiting with outward checking against a precise standard and active correction. You use your eyes and a fixed reference line to shape the body step by step.
modalities.whatYouDo: A teacher first shows you a short form and photographs or marks its key postures. At home you practice in front of a mirror with a strip of tape running down it, sinking into each low stance, lining up your head, spine and hips with the tape and adjusting, for about 30 minutes, which is enough to warm the legs. Every few weeks the teacher checks your form and adds a finer detail.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who enjoy precision and visible progress and find open, inward practices too vague. It could also interest anyone who wants to work deliberately on posture.
modalities.cautions: Warm up with a few shallow stances first, aim for comfortable alignment rather than forcing joints into perfect lines, keep stances shallow if your knees, hips or back complain, get medical advice first if you have a heart or joint condition and stop if you feel chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness. If checking the mirror feeds self-criticism about your body, cover it and work by feel for a while, and anyone with a history of psychosis should get medical advice before taking up meditative movement practice.
modalities.tweet: Mirror and Plumb Line: a strip of tape down a mirror becomes your teacher as you line up head, spine and hips at every posture of a low-stance form. A proposed practice in precision.

modalities.name: The Practice Logbook
modalities.tagline: A self-led movement plan that grows weekly, tracked in a notebook.
modalities.whatItIs: The Practice Logbook is an untested idea for a self-led, progressive movement program: you follow a written twelve-week plan that adds a little time or one new movement each week, and record every session in a notebook. Progress is planned, measured and visible on the page.
modalities.coreIdea: Aletheia Coaching lets things unfold in open conversation with a coach; this goes toward a written plan, steady progression and self-direction. The logbook turns a gentle practice into a clear training project.
modalities.whatYouDo: In week one you practice three simple movements for ten minutes a day, and each week the plan adds a few minutes, a deeper stance or a new movement, until after about three months you do a 40-minute form of eight movements that leaves you pleasantly warm. After each session you write the date, the length and one line about how your body felt. Every four weeks you read back through the log and adjust the plan if needed.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who are motivated by goals and tracking and want a gentle practice that still feels like progress. It may also suit anyone who has tried meditation but missed having a plan.
modalities.cautions: Progress at the pace of your body rather than the plan, start each session with a few easy minutes, repeat a week or go back a step if anything hurts or you feel unwell, and stop if you feel chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness. Keep up any treatment you already have, and talk to a doctor first if you have a heart, joint or balance condition or a history of psychosis.
modalities.tweet: Like a training plan, but calm. The Practice Logbook would add a few minutes, a deeper stance or one new movement each week, up to a 40-minute form, with every session written down. Untested.

modalities.name: The Daily Appointment
modalities.tagline: A small group promises daily practice of one form, checking in weekly.
modalities.whatItIs: The Daily Appointment is a new concept for a small group of four to six people who make a written promise to practice the same short qigong form every day for eight weeks, with a teacher who meets the group once a week. The point is deliberate, sustained effort: keeping a daily appointment with the form, whether or not you feel like it.
modalities.coreIdea: Do Nothing meditation drops every aim, effort and method; in the opposite direction, qigong becomes a deliberate commitment kept with others and coached by a teacher. Choosing to practice on the days you would rather not is the core of it.
modalities.whatYouDo: At the first meeting the teacher teaches a 15-minute form of steady, moderate effort, and each person writes down a simple agreement naming the time of day they will do it. Every day you practice and tick a shared chart, and once a week the group meets to practice together and compare notes while the teacher corrects the form. Missed days are noted without blame, and the agreement simply carries on.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who start practices with good intentions and drop them within weeks, and who do better when others are counting on them. It could also suit friends or colleagues who want a shared commitment.
modalities.cautions: Keep the agreement kind: missed days are not failures, and nobody should practice through pain, illness or exhaustion to keep a streak. Start each round gently, adapt movements to your body, stop if you feel chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness, and get medical advice first if you have heart, joint or balance problems or a history of psychosis.
modalities.tweet: Six people, one short form, practiced daily for eight weeks, with missed days met without blame. The Daily Appointment trades willpower for shared commitment and a weekly check-in. Untested, but appealing.

modalities.name: The Shared Pole
modalities.tagline: Two people move a light pole between their palms, keeping it level.
modalities.whatItIs: The Shared Pole is a new concept for a partner practice in which two people hold a light bamboo pole between them, one end resting in each person's palms, and move together through a fixed sequence of slow steps, turns and bends without letting it tip or drop. Nothing is said: each feels the other only through the pole.
modalities.coreIdea: Metta builds warm feeling toward people held in the imagination; this moves toward a real person, sensed directly through a shared object, with no phrases and no feeling to produce. Keeping the pole level is the only goal, and it can only be done together.
modalities.whatYouDo: After learning the sequence from a teacher, you and a partner practice for about 30 minutes, standing a pole's length apart, palms flat under the ends. You take turns leading, moving slowly enough that the other can follow by feel, and when the pole tips you stop, settle and start that movement again. The effort is steady and moderate, with plenty of stepping and bending.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel awkward with words and want a simple, physical way to cooperate closely with one other person. It could also suit couples, friends or family members who would like to do something quietly together.
modalities.cautions: Use a light, smooth pole and plenty of space, and move slowly so nobody is jabbed or pulled off balance. Adapt the bends to your body, and anyone with a history of psychosis should get medical advice before starting meditative movement practice.
modalities.tweet: Can two people move as one without speaking? In The Shared Pole, a new concept, partners step and turn together while keeping a light bamboo pole level between their palms.

modalities.name: Learn, Then Pass On
modalities.tagline: Learn a short form each week, then teach it to someone.
modalities.whatItIs: Learn, Then Pass On is a new concept for learning a movement form by passing it on: each week you learn one new section of a short form from a teacher and then teach that section to one friend or family member before the next class. Explaining it, showing it and correcting someone else becomes the way you learn it.
modalities.coreIdea: Vipassana watches experience silently and alone, without trying to change it; this moves qigong into active learning with a goal and a partner: knowing a form well enough to hand it on. Teaching it forces you to know each movement properly.
modalities.whatYouDo: In a weekly class with a few others, you learn one section of an eight-part form, about five minutes of steady, moderate movement, and practice it until you can do it from memory. During the week you meet your learner for about 20 minutes, show them the section, practice it together and correct each other. At the next class you bring back any questions your learner had.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who learn best by doing and explaining, and who like a practice with a clear purpose. It could also suit anyone who wants a gentle, regular reason to spend time with a friend or relative.
modalities.cautions: Teach only what you have learned, keep corrections gentle and hands-off unless your learner agrees, adapt movements to each body, start with a few easy movements and stop if either of you feels chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness. People with joint or heart conditions or a history of psychosis should get medical advice first.
modalities.tweet: Learn a section of a movement form on Monday, teach it to a friend by Thursday. Learn, Then Pass On is a hypothetical class in which passing it on is how you learn it.

modalities.name: Two Fingers on the Wrist
modalities.tagline: Tap softly along with your resting pulse, seated or lying down.
modalities.whatItIs: Two Fingers on the Wrist is an untested idea for a seated or lying practice in which you rest two fingers on your pulse and softly tap one fingertip of the other hand in time with each heartbeat, keeping company with your heart while it is calm. Nothing is pushed, counted or measured.
modalities.coreIdea: HIIT drives the heart rate to its limit in timed bursts; this is qigong taken as far the other way as it goes, to no effort, deep calm and acceptance of the heart as it is. Attention rests on the pulse instead of chasing it.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sitting in a supported chair or lying on a bed, you find your pulse at the wrist or neck and, for about ten minutes, let one fingertip of the other hand tap lightly on your knee or the mattress with every beat. When you lose the rhythm, you simply wait until you feel the next beat and join it again. A teacher shows you once, and after that you can practice alone.
modalities.whoItsFor: People recovering from illness or living with fatigue, for whom exercise is out of reach for now, and anyone who wants to feel at ease with their own heartbeat. It could also work for people who usually notice their heart only when it is racing.
modalities.cautions: If paying attention to your heartbeat makes you anxious, rest your hand on your chest or belly instead, or stop. Anyone with a heart condition, palpitations or new, unexplained symptoms should see a doctor rather than rely on this and keep up any treatment they already have, and anyone with a history of psychosis should get medical advice before taking up meditative practice.
modalities.tweet: Your heart usually gets noticed only when it races. Two Fingers on the Wrist would change that: ten minutes seated or lying down, tapping one fingertip softly along with your resting pulse. Untested.

modalities.name: The Supported Float
modalities.tagline: A fixed, solitary floating routine in a calm, warm pool.
modalities.whatItIs: The Supported Float is a new concept for a solitary qigong-style routine done floating on your back in a warm, quiet pool with foam supports. As in qigong, body, breath and attention are regulated together through a fixed form: the arms open slowly on each in-breath and close on each out-breath, without pause, while the water holds you up.
modalities.coreIdea: Team sport is fast, crowded and full of people to react to; the reverse is stillness, solitude and a body held up by water, with nothing to chase or answer. Letting the water carry you, in the same sequence every time, is the organizing idea.
modalities.whatYouDo: At a quiet session time, you lie back in shallow, warm water with a float under your head and knees and move through the same continuous 20-minute sequence, arms, then legs, then hands and feet opening and closing in time with the breath. You keep your ears under the surface to soften the noise around you. An instructor teaches it first, and afterward you practice alone while a lifeguard watches from the side.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who are surrounded by noise and demands all day and want a completely quiet, solitary practice. It could also suit people for whom standing or kneeling is hard, since the water takes the weight.
modalities.cautions: Water always carries a risk of drowning, so practice only in shallow water with a lifeguard on duty and never alone at home or in open water; check with a doctor first if you have epilepsy, and skip it with an open wound or an ear infection. Stand up slowly at the end, since some people feel dizzy, and anyone with a history of psychosis should get medical advice before long, still meditative practice.
modalities.tweet: The Supported Float: a qigong-style routine done floating on your back in a warm pool, arms opening and closing with the breath while a lifeguard watches. A new idea for anyone who never gets a quiet moment.

modalities.name: Move, Then Stop
modalities.tagline: Each small movement is followed by a long, complete stop.
modalities.whatItIs: Move, Then Stop is an invented practice in which every small movement in a short, fixed sequence is followed by a full stop of about 30 seconds, with the body completely still. The stops, not the movements, are what you practice.
modalities.coreIdea: Endurance training means keeping going without a break; turned around, practice becomes the skill of stopping fully, again and again, at set points. Each stop is a deliberate full stop at the end of a short sentence of movement.
modalities.whatYouDo: A teacher shows you a sequence of ten gentle movements, such as raising the arms halfway, turning the head or shifting your weight, and you practice it standing or seated for about 15 minutes. After each movement you stop completely for about 30 seconds and feel the body come to rest before starting the next. Once a month you can go back to the teacher, alone or with a small group, to check the sequence.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find it hard to stop, such as those who always push on, rush between tasks or train hard, and who want to practice stopping in a simple, physical way. It could also suit anyone who wants a very gentle routine.
modalities.cautions: It is gentle, but stop any movement that causes pain, and sit down if standing still makes you light-headed. Keep up any treatment you already have, talk to a doctor if trouble resting comes with low mood or exhaustion, and get medical advice first if you have a history of psychosis.
modalities.tweet: Runners keep going. This practice is about stopping: ten gentle movements, each followed by a complete 30-second stop. Move, Then Stop is untested and suits anyone who finds it hard to pause.

modalities.name: Never Any Harder
modalities.tagline: A gentle seated form with one rule: it never gets harder.
modalities.whatItIs: Never Any Harder is a new concept for a short, gentle seated form, breath-led in the qigong way, that comes with one firm rule: it never gets longer, harder or more advanced, however long you practice it. You do the same easy movements in the same way for months or years.
modalities.coreIdea: Strength training is built on progressive overload: always a little heavier, a little more. This turns that around completely, with no effort to speak of and no progress to chase, so that doing enough, unchanged, is the whole practice.
modalities.whatYouDo: In a small seated class or at home after two or three lessons, you sit in a chair and work through the same eight small movements, such as opening the hands on an in-breath and resting them on the knees on an out-breath, for about ten minutes. When you notice the urge to do more, go deeper or add a movement, you let it pass and do exactly what the form asks. A teacher checks every few months that the form has stayed the same, not that it has improved.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who turn everything into a self-improvement project, including those used to pushing hard in the gym, and who want to practice being content with enough. It could also suit anyone with little energy who wants a practice that will never ask for more.
modalities.cautions: It is very gentle, but stop any movement that causes pain or dizziness, keep up any treatment you already have and get medical advice first if you have a history of psychosis. If not progressing brings up strong frustration or low mood, that is worth talking through with someone.
modalities.tweet: Every workout plan tells you to add weight. Never Any Harder is a proposed seated form with one rule: it never gets harder, longer or more advanced. A practice in being content with enough.

modalities.name: Self-Written Sequence
modalities.tagline: Design your own fixed sequence of simple movements, then keep it.
modalities.whatItIs: Self-Written Sequence is a proposed practice in which you build your own short movement sequence from a small menu of simple moves, write it down and then practice it unchanged, alone, every day. You are the author, the teacher and the student.
modalities.coreIdea: Animal-assisted therapy relies on a professional, a living partner and a relationship; this goes toward complete self-reliance, solitude and a structure you design yourself. Writing the form down and then sticking to it is the heart of the practice.
modalities.whatYouDo: From a printed menu of about twenty basic moves, such as arm raises, side bends, slow turns and weight shifts, you choose six to eight, put them in an order and decide on the counts and breathing for each. You write the sequence on a card and practice it alone for 15 to 20 minutes a day for at least a month before changing anything. Some people add a simple image to each move, such as pushing a cloud or lifting water.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who prefer to work things out for themselves and like owning their routine, including those who do not get on with classes or teachers. It may also suit anyone who has tried set forms and wants one that fits their own body.
modalities.cautions: Choose moves that suit your body and leave out anything that hurts, and if you have joint, heart or balance problems ask a physiotherapist to look over your sequence. Practicing alone means no one checks on you, so stop and seek medical advice if you notice unusual mental or bodily reactions, and get advice before starting if you have a history of psychosis.
modalities.tweet: Design your own practice, then stick to it. In Self-Written Sequence you pick six to eight simple moves, write them on a card and keep them unchanged for a month. An idea for anyone who dislikes classes.

modalities.name: A Spot Nobody Goes
modalities.tagline: Walk alone to a remote spot and practice a fixed form there.
modalities.whatItIs: A Spot Nobody Goes is a new concept for solitude reached by distance: once or twice a week you walk alone to one of a few out-of-the-way spots, such as the far end of a pier, a quiet hilltop or a corner of a woodland, and practice a fixed qigong-style form there before walking back. The walk out leaves company behind, and while you are there the spot is yours alone.
modalities.coreIdea: Socializing fills time with people, talk and spontaneity; this pushes qigong the opposite way, into deliberate solitude, silence and a fixed routine, found by walking away from everyone. Going somewhere nobody else goes is the organizing idea.
modalities.whatYouDo: You pick two or three remote but safe spots about 20 minutes' walk from home and go to whichever suits the day. Each time you walk there at an easy pace without stopping to chat, practice a 20-minute form learned from a teacher, stand still for a few breaths and walk home the same way. A teacher checks your form every couple of months.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who are surrounded by others all day, such as parents, carers or people in busy jobs, and rarely get real solitude. It might also appeal to introverts who want a regular, protected stretch of time alone.
modalities.cautions: Tell someone your route and when you expect to be back, check the weather, choose a spot with safe footing and a way to call for help, check with a doctor first if you have a heart, joint or balance condition and stop if you feel chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness. Solitude is restful for some and hard for others, so if it brings up loneliness or low mood, shorten it and talk to someone, and people with a history of psychosis should get medical advice before long solitary practice.
modalities.tweet: Walk twenty minutes to somewhere nobody goes, practice a quiet form there and walk home, after telling someone your route. Parents and carers, this new concept is for you: A Spot Nobody Goes.

modalities.name: Inside One Mat
modalities.tagline: A complete indoor form that never leaves a single small mat.
modalities.whatItIs: Inside One Mat is a new concept for a fixed movement form designed to fit entirely on one small mat indoors, so you can practice in a bedroom, a hospital ward or a cramped flat. Every turn, step and reach stays inside the mat, and attention turns inward rather than out to a view.
modalities.coreIdea: Nature walks are open, outdoors and full of sights and sounds; this takes qigong into a closed room and a space barely bigger than you are. Staying inside the edges is meant to train a precise, inward sense of where your body is.
modalities.whatYouDo: A teacher teaches you a 15-minute sequence of small steps, turns and reaches that all fit within a square mat, and you practice it at home with your eyes half closed in a dim, quiet room. When a foot drifts over the edge, you notice it and bring it back, and over the weeks you aim to finish with both feet where you started. The teacher checks your form every few weeks and adds a new movement when you are ready.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who have little space or cannot easily get outdoors, such as those in small flats, shared rooms or hospital, and who want a private practice at home. It could also suit anyone who likes clear limits and precise goals.
modalities.cautions: Clear the area around the mat, use a non-slip surface, keep a chair within reach and open your eyes fully if you feel unsteady. Adapt any movement that strains your joints, people with a balance disorder should check with a doctor or physiotherapist first, and anyone with a history of psychosis should get medical advice before taking up inward-focused movement practice.
modalities.tweet: Short on space? Inside One Mat is a new idea: a 15-minute movement form designed to fit entirely on one small mat, for bedrooms, shared rooms and hospital wards.

modalities.name: Move Through Your List
modalities.tagline: A steady form where each move rehearses one task of the day.
modalities.whatItIs: Move Through Your List is a new concept for a steady, fixed movement form done before the day starts, in which each of eight movements is paired with one task on your list. As you move, you picture yourself doing that task calmly and well, so the form doubles as a rehearsal of what is ahead.
modalities.coreIdea: Sensory mindfulness rests on plain, present sensing and lets experience be; this moves toward planning, imagination and deliberately shaping how you meet what is coming. The body rehearses the day, one movement and one task at a time.
modalities.whatYouDo: Before the practice you write up to eight tasks on a card, such as a hard phone call or the school run. In a small class or at home after a few lessons, you work through eight steady movements of moderate effort for about 25 minutes, bringing one task to mind with each and picturing yourself handling it calmly. You finish with a minute of standing still with no task at all.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who start the day already overwhelmed by their list and want a practice that faces it rather than escapes it. It could also suit anyone who likes combining exercise with planning.
modalities.cautions: If picturing a task brings on dread rather than calm, drop it from the form and come back to the movement, and talk to someone if dread about your days persists. Start with a couple of easy movements, adapt any that strain your joints or balance, stop if you feel chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness, and get medical advice first if you have a heart condition or a history of psychosis.
modalities.tweet: Your to-do list, rehearsed with your whole body. Move Through Your List is a concept for mornings that start behind: eight steady movements, each paired with one task you picture doing calmly.

modalities.name: Practice Unaccompanied
modalities.tagline: A slow form with no music, only the sounds of the place.
modalities.whatItIs: Practice Unaccompanied is an invented way of practicing a slow, fixed movement form with no music, no recordings and no counting aloud, wherever you happen to be. Instead of a soundtrack, whatever the place offers, such as traffic, birds, a kettle or rain, is the only accompaniment.
